name: CANDIDA MANNAN ANTIGEN, SERUM
interpretation:
RESULT IN
 pg/mL		  REMARKS COMMENTS
< 50 Negative Indicates absence of Candida mannan antigen; suggestive of absence of Invasive Candidiasis
>= 50 - < 10 Equivocal  Indicates a suspected Invasive Candidiasis and requires repeat testing after 7-10 days
>=100 Positive   Indicates absence of Candida mannan antigen; suggestive of absence of Invasive
Candidiasis

Note
1. This assay is used for the quantitative detection of Candida mannan antigen in serum samples which signifies the presence of invasive Candida infection.
2. The sensitivity can be further enhanced by combining Serum Candida mannan assay with other fungal biomarkers including Serum Galactomannan and (1,3) Beta-D-Glucan (BDG) Assay to establish the diagnosis of invasive fungal infections before onset of signs and symptoms when the antifungal therapy is most effective thereby increasing the patient survival rates.
3. These results cannot be compared with other fungal biomarkers including Serum Galactomannan and BDG Assay as its expression in serum depends upon the stages of invasive Candida infection.
4. Paired sample analysis for Candida mannan enhances the sensitivity of the assay.
5. A negative result does not rule out the diagnosis of Invasive Candida infections in high risk individuals due to its presence in low concentration and the rapid elimination of the Candida mannan antigen during infection. Such patients should be tested twice a week for early detection of the disease.
6. The sensitivity and specificity of Serum Candida mannan detection in patients with proven or probable Invasive Candidiasis ranges from 66% to 74% and 87% to 96%, respectively.
7. This assay should be used in conjunction with other diagnostic procedures such as microbiological culture, histological examination of biopsy samples and radiographic evidence to diagnose Invasiv

 

Comments
Invasive fungal infections (IFI) are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly among patients who are significantly immunosuppressed including hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, solid organ transplant recipients, and those with hematologic or immune deficiencies and AIDS. They are mainly caused by opportunistic fungal pathogens. Candida species are the fourth most common cause of all nosocomial bloodstream infections. Prognosis depends upon timely clinical recognition and prompt administration of antifungal therapy. The techniques commonly used require invasive sample collection methods, are less sensitive and require prolonged incubation times. Due to these limitations, use of fungal biomarkers, including detection of Candida mannan has emerged as useful adjunct test for early detection of Invasive Candidiasis
